notes.trap: With ANSI mode off, casting an out-of-range numeric to INT silently wraps around instead of failing or returning NULL. Out-of-range strings behave differently and return NULL.
With ANSI off, an unparseable string cast to a number returns NULL rather than raising an error. Thousands separators are not accepted, so formatted numbers silently become NULL.
A string with a fractional part is accepted, and the fraction is truncated toward zero rather than rounded. Negative values move toward zero, unlike `floor(...)`.
With ANSI off, numeric overflow wraps modulo 256. 128 becomes -128 and no error is raised.
With ANSI off, a value outside -32768..32767 wraps silently instead of erroring or returning NULL.

decimal(expr) casts to the default DECIMAL(10,0), so the fractional digits are lost. Values are rounded half-up to whole numbers, not truncated. Use `cast(...)` with an explicit precision and scale to keep decimals.
String-to-boolean casts accept more than 'true'/'false': 't', 'y', 'yes', '1' (and their negatives) are recognised case-insensitively. Any other string becomes NULL.
With ANSI off, a well-formed but impossible calendar date returns NULL instead of an error. It is not rolled over into the next month.
A numeric argument is interpreted as seconds since the Unix epoch, not milliseconds. Use `timestamp_millis(...)` for millisecond values. The result is rendered in the session time zone.
A DOUBLE converted to string uses Java formatting. Values of 1e7 or larger (and very small values) come out in scientific notation, not plain digits.
FLOAT is single precision. Widening it back to DOUBLE exposes binary rounding error that the original decimal literal did not have.
In Spark, NaN equals NaN and sorts above all other values. This differs from IEEE semantics and from many other engines.
binary(string) takes the UTF-8 bytes of the string. It does not decode hex or base64. Use `unhex(...)` or `unbase64(...)` for those encodings.
